answer: Yes. The subtext enriches the setting rather than feeling forced. The narrator’s image of keeping her father’s world “in a drawer” implies shame and compartmentalization; its eventual transformation into “a room, a warm one” makes the Porch more than a bar—it becomes an expression of belonging. Similarly, her father’s “I can if I hold on” refers literally to dancing while quietly suggesting his dependence on his daughter and community as he approaches death. These meanings emerge naturally from concrete places, gestures, and dialogue.
